property_summary: After calling endConfiguration(), the reference contract always sets configured == true for any caller/state, whereas the mutant sets configured == false for at least some inputs, so the invariant is that endConfiguration() results in configured() == true on the reference.

Calling endConfiguration() on the correct contract always results in configured becoming true (idempotent end of configuration), whereas the mutant toggles the flag so there exist inputs where configured differs after the call.

After calling endConfiguration(), the contract's configured() getter becomes true for all inputs on the reference implementation; the mutant leaves configured() unchanged (so for some inputs it remains false), causing a divergence.

For any caller, calling endConfiguration() on the correct contract returns normally and sets configured == true; the mutant instead always reverts from endConfiguration(), so configured remains false and the call does not complete.

After any call to endConfiguration(), the reference contract leaves configured == true, whereas the mutant sets configured back to false, so the property is that endConfiguration() results in configured() == true for all inputs and the mutant violates it for some input.
Only the DAO (when already set) can call setDAO to change the DAO address (i.e., if DAO != address(0) then a non-DAO caller cannot change DAO).
If configured() is true then after configuring security and flash governance, the contract's DAO remains the same as before those calls when the caller is not the current DAO.
Calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance does not change C.DAO when those calls are made by an address that is not the current DAO and DAO was nonzero beforehand.
After calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance from any caller, the contract's DAO remains equal to its value immediately before those calls.

After calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance, the DAO address is unchanged when the caller is the test contract and the contract was already configured (configured()==true).

Invariant: Calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) must never change C.DAO() when invoked by any caller (the reference leaves DAO unchanged after the call); the mutant restricts setDAO to only DAO caller and can leave DAO changed after a call path that triggers setDAO, breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and parameters, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) does not change the stored DAO address in the correct contract; the mutant's tightened setDAO restriction allows DAO to be changed by non-DAO callers in some execution paths, so DAO can differ after the call.

For every caller and parameters, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) on the correct contract does not change the DAO address (DAO remains what was set at construction); the mutant's tightened require in setDAO allows DAO to be changed by non-DAO callers during execution flow, so for some inputs DAO differs after assertGovernanceApproved and thus violates this invariant.

For all callers and inputs, invoking assertGovernanceApproved(...) on the correct contract never results in a change to the DAO storage slot (DAO remains equal to the initial DAO); the mutant's tightened require in setDAO allows an execution path where DAO is changed by a non-DAO caller during/after assertGovernanceApproved, so DAO can differ.

For every caller and inputs, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) does not change the public DAO address of C (the reference preserves DAO after the call); the mutant's tightened setDAO allow a non-DAO caller path to change DAO, so some input causes DAO() to differ after the call.
Only the original DAO address (set earlier) can change DAO later — after configuration is finished, DAO remains equal to the previously-set DAO unless msg.sender == DAO.

After configuring security and flash-governance, DAO remains equal to its pre-existing value when configure* calls are invoked by a non-DAO successful-proposal caller (i.e., these calls do not change DAO).
After calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance from a non-DAO caller, the contract's DAO address remains unchanged (cannot be set to the caller).
After calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance from any caller, the contract's DAO address is unchanged (cannot become equal to the caller's address).
After calling configureSecurityParameters and configureFlashGovernance, the contract's DAO address must not be equal to the test caller (assert(c.DAO() != msg.sender)).

Rule: Once configured by the contract (via setDAO restrictions in the reference), arbitrary callers cannot change C.DAO through any call path — the mutant removes that restriction allowing DAO to be changed by unauthorized callers during assertGovernanceApproved; therefore for some inputs DAO differs after the call.

In the correct contract, DAO cannot be changed by arbitrary callers during assertGovernanceApproved (so DAO remains equal to its initial value after any call), whereas the mutant removes setDAO's restriction allowing some callers to change DAO during assertGovernanceApproved and thus DAO may differ afterwards for some inputs.

Invariant: For any caller and inputs, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) on the correct contract never changes C.DAO() from its initial value; the mutant (which allows anyone to call setDAO) can result in C.DAO() being changed by a malicious/contractual caller during the call, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller and inputs, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) on the correct contract never changes C.DAO() from its initial value; the mutant (which allows anyone to set DAO) can have a malicious reentrant caller change DAO during assertGovernanceApproved, so after the call DAO differs.

For any caller and inputs, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) on the correct contract never changes C.DAO() from its initial value; the mutant (which removes the setDAO restriction) allows a malicious external contract called during assertGovernanceApproved to reenter and call setDAO, so DAO can differ afterwards.
It must be possible to set DAO when DAO is currently zero by calling setDAO from any caller (i.e., setDAO(address) succeeds and updates DAO when initial DAO == address(0)).

property_summary: Calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance does not change the contract's DAO from the value it had immediately before those calls (DAO remains unchanged).
Calling configureSecurityParameters then configureFlashGovernance must not change the DAO address previously set via setDAO by this contract's deployer (constructor caller).

For any call to assertGovernanceApproved(...), the contract's DAO remains unchanged (still the initially set DAO) — the mutant that forbids setting DAO when it's zero can cause DAO to become a different address after such a call for some inputs.

For any caller and parameters, after calling assertGovernanceApproved on the correct contract the DAO address remains writable from its initial zero state (i.e., setDAO can be called to change DAO from zero to a new address), whereas the mutant that forbids setting DAO when DAO==address(0) will prevent setting DAO from zero for some inputs — so the reference always allows setDAO(address) to succeed when DAO==address(0) but the mutant blocks it.

For any caller address x, when C is freshly deployed with DAO == address(this) (non-zero), calling assertGovernanceApproved(x, target, emergency) does not prevent setDAO from being callable afterward to change DAO (i.e., setDAO can still set DAO to any address); the mutant that forbids setting DAO when it's zero will break this rule for some sequences where DAO becomes address(0) during operations and then cannot be set — so the reference preserves the ability to change DAO after assertGovernanceApproved whereas the mutant can block it for some inputs.

For any caller and parameters, after calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) on a freshly deployed C (whose DAO was set to address(this) in setUp), it must always remain possible for DAO to be changed via setDAO(address) (i.e., setDAO succeeds and DAO == newAddress); the mutant that forbids setting DAO when DAO==address(0) can make setDAO revert for some inputs, breaking this property.

For any caller address and parameters, after calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) on a freshly deployed C (initialized with DAO = address(this)), the reference contract never sets DAO to address(0) as a side-effect and thus calling setDAO(newDao) from the DAO (address(this)) always succeeds to change DAO to newDao; the mutant flips the require so that when DAO == address(0) setDAO is forbidden, allowing a sequence where DAO becomes address(0) and then cannot be set, violating the rule.

property_summary: After any call to assertGovernanceApproved(from,target,emergency) the DAO address stored in C remains unchanged (setDAO does not get involuntarily altered by that call) in the reference, but the mutant that deletes governer before assigning DAO can cause DAO to be changed for some inputs (reentrant/malicious token behavior) and thus violates this invariant.

For any admissible inputs, calling assertGovernanceApproved(...) does not change C.DAO() (the DAO address remains unchanged); the mutant that deletes governer earlier can enable a reentrant token/callee to change DAO during the call and thus violate this invariant for some inputs.

For every admissible inputs, calling assertGovernanceApproved(from,target,emergency) does not change the stored DAO address in the reference contract C; the mutant that deletes governer earlier can enable a reentrant/malicious token/callee to reenter and change DAO during the call, causing DAO() to differ after the call for some inputs.

For every admissible attacker contract and parameters, a call to assertGovernanceApproved(from,target,emergency) on the correct C never changes the governer address (i.e., c.governer() remains equal to the value obtained before the call), whereas the mutant that deletes governer earlier can allow a reentrant/malicious token/attacker to change DAO during the call and thus leave governer cleared/changed — so governer() after the call stays equal to the pre-call value on the reference but can differ on the mutant for some inputs.

For all attacker contracts and inputs where C.assertGovernanceApproved is callable, calling it on the correct C never allows a reentrant callee (invoked during token.transferFrom) to change C.DAO() — i.e., DAO remains equal to its pre-call value; the mutant that deletes governer earlier can enable reentrancy to change DAO during the call and thus violates this invariant for some inputs.
